Read About Zagreb

A capital where medieval lanes, blue trams and café tables make history feel lived-in rather than displayed.

Two towns become one

Zagreb grew where two medieval settlements faced one another across a stream. Kaptol gathered around the Cathedral and its church institutions; Gradec rose behind walls on the neighbouring hill. Their rivalry shaped the narrow streets, gates and viewpoints of today’s Upper Town long before the communities were formally united.

Tkalčićeva Street follows the former stream bed between them. Walking it now, past painted façades and crowded terraces, is to trace the seam that once divided the city. Stone Gate survives as the most intimate fragment of Gradec’s defenses, while St Mark’s Square still concentrates political power around a church whose tiled roof has become Zagreb’s visual shorthand.

Zagreb reveals itself in transitions: from square to lane, ceremony to conversation, monument to café.

The deliberate Lower Town

Below the hills, 19th-century planners gave Zagreb a different rhythm. The Green Horseshoe links formal gardens, squares and cultural buildings in a sequence that feels composed without feeling rigid. King Tomislav Square announces the railway arrival; Zrinjevac softens the civic centre with plane trees and a music pavilion; the Botanical Garden turns scientific collecting into a quiet city retreat.

The Croatian National Theatre supplies the grandest interior, but Lower Town’s character is not only ceremonial. Specialty coffee bars, market-led bistros and the steady passage of trams keep its handsome blocks practical and social. The city’s celebrated café culture is less about a particular drink than the permission to stay.

A city that keeps adapting

Earthquakes forced Zagreb to reconsider many of its landmarks, including the Cathedral and parts of Upper Town. Restoration remains visible, yet the city’s response is not a frozen reconstruction. Reopened spaces, contemporary museums and New Zagreb’s broad modernist avenues extend the story south across the Sava.

The Museum of Contemporary Art makes that shift clearest: a large collection in a building designed for movement, light and the scale of the newer city. Nearby Bundek Park shows another Zagreb habit—turning generous public space into an everyday living room. Across four days, the city’s appeal lies in this continuity between old institutions and ordinary routines.
